Please stay calm, my friend. I have sent a message to the Wang family in the capital by carrier pigeon, but the journey is long, and aid may not arrive in time.

If things go awry, Master Zhang’s whereabouts are unknown—he may not be able to help. Seek Master Yan at once; he may be our only hope.

The road ahead is perilous—take care. If all fails… do not return.

— Lianbi Nanjiong
Your aid the other day was deeply appreciated, Yingzhu is truly grateful. Yet I must make another presumptuous request—if you would be so kind, I hope we may discuss it at the Qiao residence.

Confucius said:​​
"Is it not a pleasure to learn and practice what you have studied? Is it not joyful to meet friends from afar? Is it not the mark of a gentleman to remain unresented even when others do not understand him?"

​​Youzi said:​​
"A man who is filial to his parents and respectful to his elders is unlikely to defy authority. And one who does not defy authority will never stir up rebellion. A gentleman devotes himself to the root, for once the root is firm, the Way will grow. Filial piety and fraternal duty—are they not the roots of humaneness?"

​​Confucius said:​​
"Fine words and an insinuating appearance are seldom signs of true virtue."

​​Zengzi said:​​
"Each day I examine myself on three counts: Have I been faithful in serving others? Have I been trustworthy in dealings with friends? Have I practiced what I have learned?"

​​Confucius said:​​
"To govern a state of a thousand chariots, one must be diligent in affairs and trustworthy, frugal in expenditures, and kind to the people. Employ them only at the proper seasons."

​​Confucius said:​​
"A young man should be filial at home, respectful abroad, earnest and trustworthy, overflowing in love for all, but intimate only with the virtuous. Having any energy to spare, he may then study the arts."

​​Zixia said:​​
"Honor virtue over beauty; serve parents with all one’s strength; devote oneself to the ruler at the cost of life; keep faith with friends in word and deed. Even if one says he has not learned, I would call him educated."

​​Confucius said:​​
"If a gentleman lacks gravity, he will not inspire respect, and his learning will not be sound. Hold faithfulness and sincerity as first principles. Have no friends who are not your equals. When at fault, do not hesitate to correct it."

​​Zengzi said:​​
"By attending carefully to funeral rites and honoring ancestors, the people’s virtue will grow toward sincerity."

​​Ziqin asked Zigong:​​
"When our Master arrives in any state, he invariably learns its policies. Does he seek this knowledge, or is it given to him?" Zigong replied, "Our Master gains it through his warmth, honesty, courtesy, moderation, and humility. His way of seeking is different from others’ seeking."

​​Confucius said:​​
"While a man’s father lives, observe his intentions; after his death, observe his conduct. If for three years he does not alter his father’s ways, he may be called filial."

​​Youzi said:​​
"In the practice of ritual, harmony is most valued. The Way of the ancient kings was beautiful in this—great and small matters followed this principle. Yet if harmony is sought for its own sake without restraint by ritual, it cannot be achieved."

​​Youzi said:​​
"Promises that align with what is right can be kept. Respect that follows ritual keeps disgrace at bay. Those who rely on close relationships may also be relied upon."

​​Confucius said:​​
"A gentleman does not seek to fill his belly in eating, nor comfort in dwelling. He is diligent in work and cautious in speech. He keeps close to those of the Way to correct himself. Such a man may indeed be called ‘fond of learning.’"

​​Zigong asked:​​
"What do you think of one who is poor yet not servile, or rich yet not arrogant?" Confucius replied, "That is acceptable, but better still is to be poor yet joyful, and rich yet loving ritual." Zigong said, "The Book of Songs says, ‘Like cutting, like filing, like carving, like polishing’—is this what you mean?" Confucius said, "Ah, Zigong! Now I can begin to discuss the Songs with you—for when I mention the past, you grasp what is to come."

​​Confucius said:​​
"Do not worry that others do not know you; worry that you do not know others."

My Dearest,

Winter approaches, and the cold grows sharper. Our household lacks the means to buy padded clothing—please send five or six hundred coins so I may purchase cotton cloth from the East Market and sew the garments myself. This will save us much expense.

These days, banditry runs rampant. It has been too long since your last letter. Are you, alone in distant parts, able to find steady shelter? Do you have enough to eat and wear?

Do not trouble yourself overmuch about home. Our daughter has grown more sensible—she now helps by fetching silk to supplement our income. She misses you dearly and pleads daily to see her father.

Ah... even if you’ve not saved much, return home soon, if only to come back safely. We can layer our thin robes and mend the holes in our walls. Together, we will endure this winter.

Awaiting your reply with hope.

​​Urgent Dispatch​​

Jiang Huaichu has been executed by Du Yanbai of the Imperial Guard. His sword and a manual of esoteric laws remain. An ancient alchemy formula is hidden in Qingping Village—retrieve it swiftly. Generous reward guaranteed.

​​— Chamber of Commerce, 29th Day​

​​Letter to Nameless Brother​​

My Dearest Brother,

Ten years have passed since we last met, yet I still remember our farewell in your hometown as if it were yesterday.

That night, when I could not find you after a long search, I visited your home. Your mother graciously descended to the Yellow Springs to seek you in my stead, while your sister-in-law and siblings... entertained me before joining your parents. A rather dull affair. Brother, why did you not accompany them?

Since you chose not to go then, you may come to Qingping Village to find me now. I have sent my most promising disciple to deliver this letter—do not delay when you arrive. The matter between us remains unsettled.

With timeless regards.

​​Letter to a Young Friend​​

Dear Friend,

Though we parted but a short time ago, I hear you have already journeyed to Cheng’an—no doubt your martial arts have progressed further. Truly, the younger generation cannot be underestimated.

Yet regarding the two conflicting energies within you, I must offer counsel: For most martial artists, reaching a level like Hall Master Deng’s is already a rare feat. If you seek to advance further, you must first resolve the mutual dissipation of these two forces within your body.

Among the world’s martial traditions, the Taihe School is renowned for its balance and purity of inner energy. Should you seek this method, go to ​​Taihe Mountain​​—but do not visit the front halls. Seek instead the ​​"Hidden Immortal Crag"​​ on the mountain.

With respect,

My Dearest Friend,

I have arrived in Hangzhou and paid my respects to a senior official at the prefectural office. By chance, I was assigned to patrol duties within the city. Though pursuing the Huantang Gang has proven troublesome, I am devoting my full effort to the task.

Should your travels bring you to Hangzhou, do seek me out. I will host a banquet in your honor—to repay the kindness you showed me when you aided me at Taihe Mountain.

With gratitude,
​​Qi Dingyuan​

Letter to Younger Brother Zhong​​

To My Dearest Brother Zhong,

Since the Lianhuan Stronghold rose outside our town, Cheng'an has been caught in turmoil. As the Ximen family holds its current position, we can no longer remain untouched by the chaos. Though you have never sought to inherit the family’s responsibilities, in these perilous times, the survival of the Ximen lineage must take precedence. For now, I will deal with the Lianhuan Stronghold as best I can.

Should the worst come to pass and I fall, it will fall upon you to carry on the Ximen name.

The sea and sky stretch endlessly before me—my thoughts linger with you.

Having left home years ago to trade, I now find myself trapped in Hangzhou—besieged by desperate refugees and roaming bandits. My wealth is exhausted, and my only choice is to risk death by fleeing the city.\n\nShould misfortune befall me, I pray a kind soul will deliver this letter to the Zhang family of Linchuan Village. A generous reward awaits.

Though we must now part, I beg of you this as you leave—
Do not betray tonight’s moon, nor regret today’s vows.
If by high noon tomorrow, you do not come to redeem me…
Then it was simply fate’s cruelty to sever our bond in this life.
Grant me but this—to seek this love again in the next.

Since my decision to mobilize troops without orders, I have known the shipyard affair was but a trap—a vile plot by treacherous ministers to force my defiance, fabricate crimes, and seize the wealth my family accumulated over generations...

Yet I could not stand idle while these villains slaughtered the innocent. Thus I walk into the tiger’s maw—trading the Shen fortune and my life for the survival of thousands of shipbuilders and refugees!

This path was mine alone. Only my daughter Mengqiu, young and blameless, weighs on my conscience. I implore you: take her far from this den of vipers. A life wandering the world is better than sharing her father’s fate...

With tear-stained cheeks, I kneel in final entreaty—
Do not refuse this dying man’s plea.

​​Message from Sun Cha​​

After these events, Taihe Mountain is no longer safe. I will escort Master Qianlong back to the Tide-listening Pavilion in Qiantang to seek Master Lu's counsel. Your repeated rescues are beyond gratitude. We part ways here—until we meet again in the rivers and lakes.

​​— Sun Cha​

The disgraced court official Zhu Danyang is currently hiding in the Taihe Mountain region. Seize this opportunity during the relief efforts to covertly extract him back to the capital.

If complications arise, do not hesitate to eliminate him—Taihe Mountain’s interests are secondary to this mission.

House sold, debts unpaid, I fled south,

Brush poised to write, yet tears fall first—my hand trembles.

I know my time has come. Each thought of this wracks me with unbearable grief.

Since we bound our hair as husband and wife, our years together have shone like strung pearls. Do you remember our first meeting? You astride your horse, whip in hand, galloping through the rivers and lakes—what dazzling spirit! Through hardship, you never wavered. Even when my past brought Wang Saoting's wrath upon you, imprisoning you in that village, you remained my spring sun and autumn moon—never a word of resentment.

Now this illness grips me. Medicine fails. Life and death follow Heaven's will—we cannot force it.

Guoguo is still young. You must guide her carefully: temper kindness with discipline. If she grows to fulfillment, I may close my eyes in peace beneath the Nine Springs.

—Tang Lanyue's last words

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment states:
"Precepts, meditation, wisdom—even lust and rage—
all are sacred practice."

For ten years, this dull monk contemplated
"form is emptiness,"
yet failed to grasp the Zen koans
in Miss Xiaodie’s every word.

Today, my disciple copied the Lotus Sutra—
but slipped in a line from the Platform Sutra:
"The Dharma dwells in the world,
awakening never leaves it."

In that instant, enlightenment struck.
I return to lay life—
where wine and meat become offerings,
and painting my love’s brows is chanting scripture.

My gratitude:
—to the Buddha for ferrying me this far,
—to you for the thunderclap that woke me.

The rivers and lakes stretch wide—
we part here.

Respectfully,
​​Huiji​
